paper_title: P$^2$-MOPD: Accelerating Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation via Parameter Priors

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation consolidates expert capabilities by supervising student-generated trajectories, whereas task arithmetic offers a training-free alternative through linear parameter combinations. We view the linear combination of student and expert parameters as a single differentiable model and propose P$^2$-MOPD, which jointly optimizes the mixing coefficients and the student weights under the same on-policy distillation objective. Unlike task arithmetic, which stays within the span of the frozen student and expert parameters for any choice of merging coefficients, P$^2$-MOPD keeps the student trainable, so the experts act as parameter priors without confining it to this span. Across four domains at 1.7B and 4B scales, P$^2$-MOPD achieves faster and more balanced recovery than MOPD from the same initialization, surpassing its final average recovery in half the training steps. At the end of training, our 1.7B model reaches 94.7% average recovery, versus 80.9% for MOPD.

Introduction Frontier large language models are increasingly built by training separate domain experts, often with domain-specific reinforcement learning (Wang et al., 2026), and then consolidating them into single generalist. Ideally, the consolidated model retains the capability of every expert, rather than trading one domain for another. Because MOPD benefits from supervising the students own behavior, its pipeline is heavy. Every step samples rollouts from the student and runs each teacher over them with teacher forcing to obtain token-level labels, and the student must approach each teachers performance through many such steps. Prior work has also found that MOPD does not recover all domains evenly (Kim et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026). Even when it starts from merge of the experts, it can leave one domain far behind, and continued distillation can erode capability that the merge already had. The other common way to consolidate experts is model merging. Task arithmetic (Ilharco et al., 2023) adds weighted sum of the experts task vectors to the base model without any training. Because P2-MOPD: Accelerating Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation via Parameter Priors the behavior of the merged model is never supervised, its quality is not guaranteed. In our experiments, for instance, uniform merge recovers less than half of the gap between the base model and the teachers  (Table 1)  . Task arithmetic falls short on its own, but its partial success is informative. If training-free linear combination of the experts already recovers part of their capabilities, their parameters encode useful prior for the consolidated model. We take this observation one step further. linear combination of the base student and the frozen experts is itself single model, differentiable in both its mixing coefficients and the students weights, and can therefore be trained end to end under the MOPD objective. Viewed this way, the experts no longer serve only as an initialization or one-off merge but act as parameter priors throughout training, so the student need not climb the whole way to each teacher on its own. Based on this view, we propose P2-MOPD (Parameter-Prior MOPD; Figure 2). It keeps the MOPD loss and its supervision on the students own trajectories, but parameterizes the student as linear combination of its own trainable weights and the frozen expert parameters (Equation (4)). The student thus receives two kinds of guidance from the experts under single loss: their logits supervise its outputs, as in MOPD, and their parameters enter its weights through the mixing coefficients, which the on-policy loss updates together with the student weights. Unlike task arithmetic, P2-MOPD keeps the base students weights fully trainable, so the consolidated model is not confined to the span of the student and expert parameters. Such confinement would be restrictive, since task vectors of separately trained experts interfere with each other (Yadav et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2024), and with only directions per module the merged model can trade one domain against another but cannot make adjustments that none of the experts contains. In P2-MOPD, the mixing coefficients move the model along expert-derived directions and the weights adapt it beyond them. The closest prior work, IM-MOPD (Kim et al., 2026), also reuses the expert parameters but merges task vectors into the student at fixed points according to an external validation rule, whereas P2-MOPD learns the combination continuously from the distillation gradient. To understand why learning the combination helps, we project each models change onto the task vectors (Section 4.3). MOPD from the merged start moves the student along most task vectors but hardly along that of the expert whose domain it leaves behind. P2-MOPD moves an order of magnitude farther along this direction, and across methods the recovery of that domain tracks the movement. The learnable coefficients thus make reachable teacher-aligned direction that student weight-only updates do not take, while the weights adapt the student outside the span of the task vectors, so the two channels divide the work. Across four domains (medicine, law, finance and instruction following) at two scales, P2-MOPD is both faster and more balanced than MOPD from the same merged start (Section 4.2). After half the training steps, it already exceeds the final average recovery of MOPD at lower wall-clock cost (Figure 1), and at the end of training it raises worst-domain recovery from below half to nearly 90%. Learning the mixing coefficients alone, inside the span, falls far short, so both the expert prior and the freedom to leave its span are needed (Section 5). Our contributions are as follows. We propose P2-MOPD, which treats linear combination of the student and frozen experts as single model and trains its weights and mixing coefficients jointly under the MOPD objective (Section 3). Student weight-only MOPD updates barely move along the direction of the lagging expert; the learnable coefficients make this direction reachable, while the weights adapt the student beyond the task-vector span (Section 4.3). At two scales, P2-MOPD surpasses the final average recovery of MOPD in half the training steps and raises worst-domain recovery from below 50% to nearly 90% (Sections 4.2 and 5). 2. Related Work Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation. On-policy distillation (OPD) (Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025; Yang et al., 2025; 2026a; Li et al., 2026; Fu et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026; Xing et al., 2026; Kang et al., 2026) supervises the student with teacher feedback on its own trajectories and has become dense-reward alternative to reinforcement learning in LLM post-training. MOPD (Ma et al., 2026a) extends OPD to consolidating several RL-trained domain experts by routing each prompt to the teacher of its domain, and is used in recent frontier technical reports to consolidate domain experts into one model (Xiaomi LLM-Core Team, 2026b;a; DeepSeek-AI, 2026; Yang et al., 2026b; NVIDIA, 2026; Kimi Team, 2026). Follow-up work refines which teacher supervises which token and how strongly, through budget balancing across domains (Gao et al., 2026), label-free token routing (Xu et al., 2026), or soft-prompt teachers (Ma et al., 2026b). These methods improve the supervision but treat the student as plain set of weights. Closest to ours, IM-MOPD (Kim et al., 2026) shows that the expert parameters themselves also help: it initializes the student by task arithmetic and periodically merges task vectors of under-recovered domains back into it. However, these merges are rule-based and rely on an extra validation signal rather than the distillation gradient. P2-MOPD instead treats the linear combination of trainable student parameters and frozen expert parameters as single differentiable model, 2 P2-MOPD: Accelerating Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation via Parameter Priors jointly optimizing the student weights and expert mixing coefficients throughout training under the same on-policy objective. Model Merging. Model merging combines experts in weight space without training, for example by task arithmetic (Ilharco et al., 2023) and its interference-reducing variants (Yadav et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2024). Because good fixed coefficients are hard to choose, another line learns them: AdaMerging (Yang et al., 2024) fits taskor layer-wise coefficients by entropy minimization on unlabeled test data, and subsequent methods learn them from task data, expert logits or expert activations (Zhang et al., 2024; Gauthier-Caron et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025). Other work interleaves merging with training as discrete step between phases (Choshen et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2025; Shen et al., 2025). Together, these works show that trained expert parameters can be combined into reasonable model even without training. They still treat merging as an operation that outputs model, either offline or between training phases. Our view is different: since task arithmetic is linear and fully differentiable function of its coefficients, the combination of student and expert parameters can be treated as one model. P2-MOPD trains this model inside MOPD, so the expert parameters serve as prior and the on-policy objective updates both the mixing coefficients and the student weights, without confining the student to the span of the task vectors. 3. Method P2-MOPD rests on simple view. linear combination of model parameters is itself single model, whose forward pass uses only the composed weights, and the composition is differentiable in its mixing coefficients. P2-MOPD therefore reparameterizes the MOPD student as trainable student weights plus learnable combination of frozen expert weights, and jointly optimizes the student weights and the mixing coefficients under the on-policy distillation objective (Figure 2). The experts thus guide the student in two ways: their logits supervise its behavior, and their weights serve as parameter priors. Experimental Setup Models and data. We follow the protocol of IMMOPD (Kim et al., 2026) at two scales, Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-1.7B. The base θ0 is the general SFT reference model of that work, and at each scale four domain teachers (medical, law, finance, instruction following) are finetuned from the same θ0, so the task vectors τk = θk θ0 are well defined. The domains are evaluated on MedQA, CaseHOLD, FinQA and IFBench. We omit the fifth domain, τ 2-bench (Barres et al., 2025), because its user simulator requires paid commercial LLM API. Every training batch contains 128 prompts, 32 from each domain, and each prompt is distilled from the teacher of its domain. Teacher provenance, prompt pools and test splits are given in Section C. Methods. MOPD (TA init) is the primary control: MOPD from the uniform TA merge (λk = 0.25), that is, P2-MOPD with the mixing coefficients α frozen at λ (the ηα = 0 corner of Algorithm 1). MOPD starts from θ0 and MOPD (SFT warm-up) from an SFT warm-up on teacher samples. Open-MOPD (Gao et al., 2026) adds per-domain budget balancing, and IM-MOPD (Kim et al., 2026) periodically merges the task vectors of under-recovered domains into the student; both start from the same merge. P2-MOPD uses module-wise granularity unless stated otherwise. Training and evaluation. All experiments run on eight GPUs (Section F). Every run trains for 100 steps of one rollout batch each, the training budget of IM-MOPD; we call the checkpoint at step 100 the final checkpoint. Checkpoints P2-MOPD: Accelerating Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation via Parameter Priors at steps 25, 50, 75 and 100 are scored with the official IMMOPD evaluation harness, which samples three responses per test item with evaluation seeds 42, 43 and 44 and averages their scores (avg@3; Section G). Per-domain recovery is (ssbase)/(steachersbase); the headline metric is the average recovery over the four domains, and the worst-domain recovery measures balance. Because the base-to-teacher spans differ by up to factor of three across domains, we report raw scores alongside. P2-MOPD, MOPD (TA init) and IM-MOPD are also trained with three training seeds at both scales; we report their means and standard deviations over the three training runs and compare P2-MOPD and MOPD (TA init) in pairs of runs with the same training seed. 4.2. Main Results Faster recovery. Figure 1 compares P2-MOPD with MOPD (TA init), which differs from it only in freezing the mixing coefficients α at their TA values. P2-MOPD is ahead from the first checkpoint, by +6.2 (4B) and +21.5 (1.7B) average-recovery points at step 25, and stays ahead in all 24 seed-paired comparisons (two scales, three seeds, four checkpoints; Section G). After half the training steps it reaches 92.3 (4B) and 90.5 (1.7B), already above the final average recovery of MOPD (TA init) (83.1 and 80.9) in every seed pair, and the advantage carries over to wall-clock time (Section 4.4). The two scales differ in how the gap evolves. At 4B it widens at every checkpoint, to +11.7 at the end of training. At 1.7B it emerges at the first checkpoint, and P2-MOPD continues to recover gradually. Final performance. At the end of training P2-MOPD leads at both scales in average recovery  (Table 1)  and in mean raw score, by +2.66 (4B) and +2.17 (1.7B) points (paired, three seeds); the raw gain is positive in every seed. P2-MOPD also ends well above MOPD and MOPD (SFT warm-up), and above IM-MOPD at both scales, with nonoverlapping seed ranges (93.597.2 versus 86.689.2 at 4B, 94.295.8 versus 59.077.4 at 1.7B). At 1.7B, IM-MOPDs end point depends on which domains its validation-gated rule happens to merge, and its average recovery varies by 18 points across seeds. Balanced recovery. The learned mixture is stable: after training, the mean coefficient of each teacher agrees across the three seeds to within 0.01, so the mixture is structured outcome learned from the experts and the student. It also moves away from the uniform 0.25 in consistent direction. The medical coefficient rises the most (to 0.63 at 4B and 0.65 at 1.7B, against 0.330.46 for the other three teachers; Table 9), toward the domain that MOPD (TA init) fails to recover (Section 4.3). When the weights are frozen, the coefficients have to absorb the whole update: they move much further (std over all module coefficients 0.380.40 versus 0.120.14), and some module coefficients become negative. Learned jointly with the weights, they stay moderate mixture of the experts, because the student weight channel adapts what the task-vector span cannot express. The learned coefficients are thus reproducible and interpretable by-product of training: without any validation data, they identify the teacher that the student most needs. 6. Conclusion We proposed P2-MOPD, which treats linear combination of the student and frozen experts as single model and trains its weights and mixing coefficients jointly under the MOPD objective. Across four domains at 1.7B and 4B, it surpasses the final average recovery of MOPD in half the training steps and raises worst-domain recovery from below half to nearly 90%. The gain comes from reachability. Student weight-only updates barely move along the task vector of the lagging domain, whereas one learnable coefficient per module makes this direction reachable, and the student weight channel adapts the model beyond the task-vector span. The advantage persists without merged initialization, and the learned coefficients consistently identify the teacher that the student most needs. More broadly, expert parameters need not be consumed once, as an initialization or merge. Kept as learnable priors throughout distillation, they guide where the student moves, which makes expert weights, and not only expert predictions, source of supervision for multi-teacher consolidation.
